item.title: I replaced the cloud with a spare laptop and Syncthing, and now my files sync for free
item.itunes:title: I replaced the cloud with a spare laptop and Syncthing, and now my files sync for free
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One of the great things about cloud services is that, in addition to providing a backup of your most important files, they can make them accessible on all your devices in a seamless way. A service like OneDrive integrates right into File Explorer on Windows 11, so you can see your cloud files just as if they were stored on your computer.

But what if you didn't need the cloud for that experience and you could do it yourself? It's actually much easier than you think, and you don't even need a NAS unit. All it takes is a spare laptop (or other PC) and Syncthing.

Syncthing keeps my files in sync

It's very easy to set up

If you're not familiar with Syncthing, it's a beautifully simple piece of software that keeps files in sync across multiple devices. It doesn't require a dedicated piece of hardware like a NAS or anything, either. You just install the app on the devices you want to sync, and you're mostly good to go.

The way it works is that you simply create a share in Syncthing on one of your devices, and when you do, it gives you a sharing code. You can then use that code to add the same folder on your other devices, and you can map that shared folder to a location of your choosing on your second device.

Syncthing keeps every device I own in sync without a single file ever touching a cloud server

I'm done with costly subscriptions.

By  Patrick Hearn

From that point on, the contents of that folder are always kept in sync between the two devices without you needing to do anything manually. Just add or remove files from the folder that's being synced, and they will quickly be reflected on your other devices. Because this works entirely within your local network, it tends to be pretty fast, too.

When I first heard of Syncthing, I was almost shocked at how easy it was to set up and how well it did its job.

A spare laptop makes all the difference

It's always working

Syncthing works great, but the main notable limitation is that it won't work as well if you have two devices that aren't powered on at the same time. Changes to your synced folder on one PC won't be detected by another PC if that second computer is off, and if you turn off the first PC before turning on the second one, there's no time when the folders can sync.

That's where the spare laptop comes in. Laptops are relatively low-power devices, so they can stay powered on without using too much energy. What I can do then is install Syncthing on this spare laptop, add it to the folder share, and just keep the laptop running in a corner of my house.

My entire family replaced Google Drive with Syncthing, and here's how I set it up

Bye-bye, Google Drive. Hello, private family cloud.

22
By  Yash Patel

Because this laptop is always powered on, it acts as a relay for all the changes I make to the synced folder on my other devices. What that means is that these other devices don't need to be powered on at the same time as each other; the changes will be synced to this spare laptop, and when a different device comes online, those changes are then pushed from the laptop to said device in a matter of seconds. It's surprisingly similar to using OneDrive or another cloud-based service.

Save money on the cloud

It doesn't have to be a laptop, either

There are multiple reasons to get a cloud subscription, but they can become pretty expensive, and if you only want one in order to be able to access your files across devices, you can easily save that money with a solution like this. I used a laptop for my setup, but you can easily do the same thing by installing Syncthing on a desktop computer or even a NAS unit, so you can keep files in sync your way.

Because it has a low-power processor, a laptop is a great candidate for this, but you can also use a mini PC and save even more power and space since there's no screen to account for. Set the power mode to battery saver (or similar setting on Linux), disable as many background services as possible, and you have a setup that costs nothing in terms of hardware or software, and it should only have a minimal impact on your electricity bill, too. You'll end up saving some money and all the files are directly in your control, never leaving your own network.

I self-host Syncthing to sync files between my PC, Mac, NAS, and other devices

Syncthing is a neat utility when you want multi-directional file synchronization for your home lab

4
By  Ayush Pande

What's more, you can set up multiple shares for different devices, all using the same laptop as a relay. If you want different files and folders that you want to be available on different devices, you can simply create multiple shares and have them all on that spare laptop, while only connecting the appropriate endpoints to each share.

Syncthing is great

There are plenty of free tools out there that can replace paid alternatives in one way or another, but many of them come with a learning curve that's often a deterrent to most people. Syncthing is one of those tools that's so impressively easy to use that I think everyone should give it a try. It can be incredibly useful and the time it takes to set up is no more than a few minutes in total. You can't say that about a lot of software.

item.title: Your Windows SSD is full because of these 6 folders — and most of them are safe to empty
item.itunes:title: Your Windows SSD is full because of these 6 folders — and most of them are safe to empty
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I can't recall the last time I manually downloaded hundreds of gigabytes on my PC (apart from a game or two). And yet, I've seen my disk fill up behind my back despite not having installed or downloaded anything unusual. Tens of gigabytes have disappeared into folders I barely remember, and it's not even all junk.

Making matters more confusing is that I can't just find the biggest folder and hit Delete before calling it a day, either. It's important to know exactly which folders on your Windows PC can keep growing, which files Windows considers temporary, and what it expects you to clean through its own tools.

The clutter that keeps growing on your PC isn't all deletable, sadly. There's a lot there that you've got to keep around, ranging from folders you can delete recklessly to those you shouldn't touch with a ten-foot pole.

7 tips to efficiently organize your drive space

Keeping your drive clean and neatly organized will help you find your files faster and improve the PC performance.

3
By  Claudiu Andone

Temp folders are the easiest cleanup win

Delete the contents, but not the folder

Temp folders on Windows exist for programs that need a place to dump the files they expect to use temporarily. However, some apps mistake "temporary" for "until retirement." By default, Windows has two Temp locations — a user temp folder and a system-wide one. The former can be accessed by typing in %TEMP% into the Run dialog box (Win + R), and the latter is located at C:\Windows\Temp.

Both of these Temp locations are pretty easy to clean up, because you can safely delete the contents of both folders. There's a safeguard in place where files that are currently in use will simply refuse to be deleted. So, if Windows says a file is in use, just skip it, which is the whole point.

It's imperative you don't delete the Temp directories themselves, though. All the content you can delete is inside the folder, so select what's in there and clear it out. In doing so, you may recover anything from a few hundred megabytes to several gigabytes if you're doing this cleanup for the first time.

I partitioned my OS drive years ago: Here's why I regret it

Partitioning my OS drive has come with some drawbacks in the long-term

43
By  Megan Ellis

Your browser cache, too, eats your storage

You can delete it freely, but it's a regular job

Chrome, Edge, Brave, or Firefox all maintain caches because downloading the same images, scripts, fonts, and other website assets every single time would be inefficient. It makes sense in practice, so cache trades storage for speed by keeping a local copy of things your browser can reuse. On the flip side, leaving it alone can make the convenience turn into a chunky pile of files.

It's safe to clear the browser cache — cached web content, by nature, is disposable, after all. When you delete it, the browser will just rebuild it when you browse the next time. The catch, of course, is that websites will take a little longer to load the first time afterward, which is the cache rebuilding itself.

Contrary to popular belief, cookies, saved passwords, autofill information, and site data that's stored in your browser are not cached files. As such, make sure you are clearing the cache rather than every other category in your browser's "delete browsing data" screen. If your goal is to reclaim storage without disrupting your browsing life, the cache is the door you want.

Your browser has a secret config page, here's how to access it and what to change

Watch out for the hidden menu under the hood!

By  Abhinav Raj

The Windows Update cache can get surprisingly large

It's safe to clear, but don't delete it like ordinary junk

I have my fair share of complaints about Windows Update, and its cache is only one of them. By default, Windows Update downloads installation files into C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download before they are needed. After an update finishes, fails, or gets superseded, these files can stick around, though. All the while, Windows tends to carry on as though nothing happened. If you're wondering, this disposable working data, not your installed updates.

You can clear the contents of this folder, but it's important to go through the right door when beginning the process. Windows Update may have some of these files open, so manually deleting them while the service is active can produce errors, or it will leave you fighting permissions for no good reason. The clean and correct approach is to just use Disk Cleanup or Storage Sense. Alternatively, for the completely manual route, you can just stop the Windows Update service first and then clear the Download folder.

Remember to delete the contents of the SoftwareDistribution\Download folder rather than the folder itself.

There's no prize for making Windows Update angry, though. Clearing its downloaded cache won't uninstall Windows updates, and Windows can simply download what it needs again. The upside, though, is reclaimed storage, all of which you get without disturbing the OS itself.

I changed one Windows 11 setting in Storage Sense, and freed 30GB without breaking anything

I should've done this years ago.

2
By  Hamlin Rozario

Windows.old is the biggest easy win

Delete it through Windows and reclaim tens of gigabytes immediately

After a Windows upgrade or reinstall, the OS creates C:\Windows.old. It does so in order to preserve the previous installation so you can roll back if the new version misbehaves in any way whatsoever. This makes it extraordinarily useful, but only immediately after an upgrade. Once you know you're keeping the new installation, Windows.old can be extraordinarily wasteful, and depending on the upgrade, it can consume tens of gigabytes.

As such, you can remove it, but it's important to know how. Don't just open Explorer, select the Windows.old folder, and send it straight to the Recycle Bin. Even though this folder is from a previous installation, Windows still treats it as protected system data. As such, use Disk Cleanup, and select the previous Windows installation option instead. Windows very helpfully handles the permissions and associated cleanup for you.

There's also a built-in expiration date for this. Windows normally removes the previous installation after about ten days. If your new installation is stable, and you have no intention of rolling it back, then removing it sooner can get you back a significant chunk of storage without sacrificing anything too important.

I used older Windows versions, and I think nostalgia has blinded us

Windows 11 is actually an improvement

19
By  João Carrasqueira

WinSxS looks guilty, but leave it alone

Let DISM do the housekeeping

One of Windows' biggest optical illusions is C:\Windows\WinSxS. Explorer can report a frightening number, making it look like the operating system has been hoarding duplicates for no apparent reason at all. However, much of that apparent size is due to hard links, so the folder's reported size doesn't actually represent the storage consumed, despite what Explorer might seem to suggest.

It's never a good idea to manually delete files from WinSxS, so, don't. Windows uses this component store for updates, repairs, enabling features, and maintaining different versions of system components. Removing files from the WinSxS folder can break servicing and leave Windows unable to repair or update itself properly.

While we’re here, skip deleting your Prefetch files. This is a recommendation that's echoed everywhere, but Windows manages it itself, and wiping it can actually slow down your next few launches.

However, if you do need to trim it, you can reliably use Windows' own servicing tools. For this, run an elevated PowerShell or Command Prompt window (run as Administrator). Then, type in the following line of code:

DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanupDoing this removes superseded components that Windows no longer needs. The bottom line here is that WinSxS can always be cleaned, but you should always let Windows itself decide what is disposable and when it is safe to remove.

I fixed Windows 11 File Explorer lag by disabling this legacy service

A quarter-century old service we no longer need.

13
By  Samarveer Singh

Windows Installer isn't a junk drawer

It's best just to steer clear entirely

Another folder that practically begs to be deleted is C:\Windows\Installer. A quick look will show you that it keeps ballooning and consumes several gigabytes, and it contains files with some rather cryptic names, and offers almost no indication why it exists. What's important, however, is to resist the temptation to do so. This is where Windows Installer keeps cached installation packages and patches.

These files can come in handy later when an application needs to repair itself, apply another update, or uninstall cleanly. The nasty part is that even if you delete one of these massive files, you may not notice anything immediately — the breakage could arrive months later. By that time, you'd have forgotten touching the Installer folder.

Since Windows can't assume that these packages are expendable, there's no general-purpose cleanup button for this folder. The best course of action when dealing with this folder is to leave it alone. If storage is tight, uninstall the applications you no longer use, and just let Windows and those apps manage their installer data. After all, a mysterious folder is still better than a mysteriously broken application.

13
By  Abhinav Raj

A cleaner PC starts with knowing when to stop

An enormous folder doesn't always mean something is wrong — Windows could just be doing its job the way it should.

Freeing up storage on Windows is less about becoming ruthless with the Delete key and more about understanding what your operating system is doing in the first place. By itself, if a folder is enormous, it doesn't mean that something has gone wrong. Sometimes it just means that Windows is doing its job the way it's supposed to, even if it does so like a squirrel preparing for winter.

As a matter of principle, storage cleanup should always leave your PC more predictable, not less so. Reclaiming space shouldn't result in a full afternoon of troubleshooting, after all. That's why it's important to know which files are disposable, which ones need Windows to handle them, and which ones are better left alone. Your SSD will thank you, and your future self, especially so.

I can't recall the last time I manually downloaded hundreds of gigabytes on my PC (apart from a game or two). And yet, I've seen my disk fill up behind my back despite not having installed or downloaded anything unusual. Tens of gigabytes have disappeared into folders I barely remember, and it's not even all junk.

Making matters more confusing is that I can't just find the biggest folder and hit Delete before calling it a day, either. It's important to know exactly which folders on your Windows PC can keep growing, which files Windows considers temporary, and what it expects you to clean through its own tools.

The clutter that keeps growing on your PC isn't all deletable, sadly. There's a lot there that you've got to keep around, ranging from folders you can delete recklessly to those you shouldn't touch with a ten-foot pole.

Delete the contents, but not the folder

It's imperative you don't delete the Temp directories themselves, though. All the content you can delete is inside the folder, so select what's in there and clear it out. In doing so, you may recover anything from a few hundred megabytes to several gigabytes if you're doing this cleanup for the first time.

Partitioning my OS drive has come with some drawbacks in the long-term

43

Your browser cache, too, eats your storage

You can delete it freely, but it's a regular job

Chrome, Edge, Brave, or Firefox all maintain caches because downloading the same images, scripts, fonts, and other website assets every single time would be inefficient. It makes sense in practice, so cache trades storage for speed by keeping a local copy of things your browser can reuse. On the flip side, leaving it alone can make the convenience turn into a chunky pile of files.

It's safe to clear the browser cache — cached web content, by nature, is disposable, after all. When you delete it, the browser will just rebuild it when you browse the next time. The catch, of course, is that websites will take a little longer to load the first time afterward, which is the cache rebuilding itself.

item.itunes:title: Your mesh Wi-Fi's real problem is printed on the manufacturer's own website
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Netgear sells a mesh system that costs more than most laptops. Then it explains on its own website why the wireless half of it is the weak part. Eero says a gentler version of the same thing.

Now, we at XDA have already realized this case through our own experiences. We have gone from your mesh Wi-Fi not being the problem to the wired upgrade your walls already have. So I decided to skip the reviews this time: no more of 'using MoCA adapters, then running tests, and reading speeds'. As I said, you will find a plethora of information around those, already at XDA.

With this article I planned to read the manufacturers instead. It turns out that Netgear, Eero, Apple, and Cloudflare all have published explanations that point to the same underlying problem. And yet, most people don't realize the extent of this problem.

MoCA adapters beat my mesh Wi-Fi system, and I wish I'd tried them first
9
By  Rich Edmonds

A second mesh node doesn't hand out a second microphone

It just puts another mouth on the one already in the room

Let's start with the part the reviews need to skip. A Wi-Fi channel behaves like a room with one microphone. Everyone hears everything, and the one who holds it gets to talk. The rule has a name: carrier sense with collision avoidance, and its job is to make sure one radio at a time transmits in a given space.

Your laptop is in that room. So is your phone, the doorbell camera, every satellite in your mesh, and your neighbor's router if it landed on your channel. Speed describes how fast you talk while you hold the microphone. It says nothing about how long you wait to get it. A weak, far-off device talks slowly to be understood, so it holds the microphone longer.

So a third satellite doesn't hand out another microphone. It puts another mouth on the one already there, and XDA's reporting on what extra satellites do to throughput lands in the same place. What nobody explains is who those satellites are talking to while they hold it.

Wi-Fi 7 borrows a second microphone from a room nobody has walked into

And your next laptop is going to want it back

A satellite's backhaul is the link carrying its traffic back to the router, and it has one job. Hear what the router said, then say it again for the far end of the house. On a dual-band kit, it does that on the band your devices already use, so every packet takes the microphone twice.

Eero, which sells wireless mesh, puts it in its own key takeaways: wiring the nodes to the router instead of letting them talk wirelessly frees up bandwidth and improves speed, stability and latency. That is a company describing the cost of its own default setup.

Netgear's Wi-Fi 7 answer is real, and its page is the only marketing I've read that argues with itself. The Orbi 970 gives backhaul a dedicated 5 GHz radio, then uses Multi-Link Operation to bond it with 6 GHz for up to 10 Gbps, against roughly 2 Gbps a generation ago. That 6 GHz radio carries about 11.5 Gbps of capacity, and Netgear reuses most of it for backhaul because hardly anyone owns Wi-Fi 7 devices yet.

That's a second microphone borrowed from a room nobody has walked into. It works because you haven't bought the hardware that would fill the room. So the mechanism is on the record and the fix has a shelf life.

The check that settles it is five browser tabs and no purchase

A speed test measures how fast you talk, never how long you wait

A speed test pulls one big file while nothing else is happening and reports how fast that went. That's the microphone-holding number. The thing you actually feel — the call that breaks up when somebody starts a backup — is how often you get a turn.

Apple built a measurement for that and ships it with every Mac. It grades a connection Low, Medium or High, and calls Low the state where video calls and gaming turn unreliable as soon as another device starts downloading. That's the symptom, written down by the company that made the laptop.

The metric under that label isn't an Apple house standard. It's round-trips per minute, and it lives in a Standards Track proposal at the IETF co-written by Apple engineers, which puts numbers on the scale. About 300 round-trips per minute is the floor for an acceptable phone call. Around 1,000 is where a call stops being merely fair. Low, Medium and High never gave you that.

You don't need a Mac for the same idea. Cloudflare's browser test scores loaded latency — your ping while the connection is busy — next to download speed, then grades the result for streaming, gaming and calls. Open the page it points you at for a 'poor network' score and the first suggestion is a wired connection.

Run the browser test twice. Once beside your router, once in the room that annoys you. If the download figure barely moves and the loaded latency triples, your devices are fine and the hop behind them isn't.

That's the diagnosis. The cure is where I have to be honest about what a wire can't do.

A wire in the wall doesn't reach every room

And it was never going to fix a weak signal to your phone

Here’s the catch nobody talks about. Wiring a satellite’s backhaul, either with Ethernet or the coax already in your walls, gives it a dedicated line to the router. It stops competing with your devices for wireless airtime. But it never changes the final wireless hop to your phone, so a weak room can still stay weak.

The alliance behind networking over coax rates the MoCA backhaul case at up to 2.5 Gbps, with less than 2.5 ms of average one-way latency across 400 to 1,675 MHz. Then comes the list nobody puts in the ad.

What it takes

Why it matters

A pair of MoCA 2.5 adapters

One at the router, one at the satellite

A splitter that passes 1,675 MHz

Older ones stop near 1,000 MHz, just under the band

A point-of-entry filter

Keeps your traffic in your walls and off the street

A coax outlet in the right room

The part nobody sells you

Coax is a shared medium too, so what you get is a second room with one microphone in it, not a private line per device. The faster version isn't coming either, and XDA has watched MoCA 3.0 fail to arrive for years.

Notice what Netgear puts on the back of its Wi-Fi 7 flagship anyway. Ten-gigabit Ethernet ports, and its own suggestion to use them as backhaul. The best wireless backhaul on the market ships with a wire.

The companies selling the best wireless systems have already told you this

None of this is on the box, and all of it is on the product pages you'd read before buying. Netgear's own capacity figures, Eero's own best practice, and the first line of advice in that last Cloudflare screenshot all point the same way.

So, before another node goes into the cart, open the tabs. If the download figure holds up and the responsiveness doesn't, a new satellite is one more mouth on the same microphone.

item.title: The Steam Deck 2 is still in the works as Valve weighs "how and when" to launch it
item.itunes:title: The Steam Deck 2 is still in the works as Valve weighs "how and when" to launch it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Valve says it still wants the Steam Deck 2 to offer a clear performance upgrade.
  • Release timing will depend on market conditions and rising component prices, says Valve.
  • Don't expect the Steam Deck 2 to drop soon; Valve will likely wait years to avoid delays and high costs.

As far as handhelds that aren't the Switch 2 go, the SteamOS-powered Steam Deck is by far the most popular out there.

For years, Valve has teased that a successor to the original Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED is in the works, but given Steam Machine's and Steam Frame's expensive price tag, it wouldn't be that surprising to hear that the company has at least temporarily put the Steam Deck 2's development on hiatus. At the very least, it would make sense for Valve to release a cheaper-to-manufacture, more incremental update to the handheld, similar to Asus' ROG Ally X20.

However, in a recent IGN interview, Valve developer Pierre-Loup Griffais said Valve's plans haven't changed. The company still wants the Steam Deck 2 to offer a meaningful upgrade to the OG Steam Deck.

"We've talked before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, and I think we're still looking at it in the same way," said Griffais. He added that Valve is watching current market conditions to figure out "how and when" it should drop the Steam Deck 2.

The Steam Deck 2 is still coming

We likely won't see the new handheld for at least a few more years

Valve hasn't shared any concrete information about the Steam Deck's successor and has only said the company is "hard at work" on the handheld. Beyond that, Valve has also said it wants the Steam Deck 2 to be a meaningful power upgrade without sacrificing battery life.

A few months ago, Valve increased the cost of the Steam Deck OLED 512GB from $550 to $790, while the 1TB configuration jumped from $650 to $950. At the time, Valve said the price increase was due to higher memory and storage costs.

While memory prices likely aren't returning to where they were a few years ago, Valve is likely waiting for a slowdown or minor dip in the skyrocketing costs before releasing the Steam Deck 2. The company also likely wants to avoid revealing the handheld nd then repeatedly delaying it, as it was forced to do with the Steam Machine.

With this in mind, it'll probably be a few years until the Steam Deck 2 is released.

The Steam Deck's price has increased from $549 to $789 as hardware woes continue

The shortages have ended, for a high price.

item.title: Fedora 45's beta is now available to download, and there's good news for fans of GNOME and KDE
item.itunes:title: Fedora 45's beta is now available to download, and there's good news for fans of GNOME and KDE
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Fedora 45 Beta is available now; full release due Oct 20.
  • Includes GNOME 51 or KDE Plasma 6.7, bundling Linux 7.2.
  • RPM now rejects unsigned packages by default; Atomic ISOs use image-builder.

With Fedora 45's release on the horizon, it's time to give it a test run to see if everything's working alright. Red Hat has released a public beta for the new version of its operating system, and there are some nice features to check out whether you prefer GNOME or KDE.

Fedora 45 Beta introduces GNOME 51 and KDE Plasma 6.7 into the mix

Something new, regardless of which you prefer

As spotted by Linuxiac, Fedora 45 Beta is now ready for you to download and try. The biggest difference you'll note is the upgrade in desktop environments. If you prefer using the stock version of Fedora, you'll get access to GNOME 51; if you're more of a fan of its KDE spin, you'll find yourself at the helm of Plasma 6.7. Regardless of which one you pick, you'll get Linux 7.2 bundled in.

Other than the obvious changes, there are a few nuances under the hood that are worth noting. First of all, RPM will now reject unsigned packages by default; you'll need to tell it to proceed if you want to download one. Fedora Atomic ISOs have moved from lorax to image-builder, and you can install them remotely using the Anaconda WebUI. Finally, DNF5 will no longer automatically change vendors during an upgrade.

The full version of Fedora 45 is scheduled to release on October 20th, but if you don't want to wait that long, pop over to the Fedora 45 Beta summary. There, you can grab the ISO of your choice and read the full patch notes for Fedora 45. As you might imagine, there are plenty of changes in this new version of Fedora, so it may be worth giving the changelog a quick once-over to ensure you're up-to-date on the changes (or lack thereof) for your favorite tools.

Fedora's Atomic desktop model is quietly becoming the future of Linux for normal people

Users don't need to worry about breaking their system anymore.

item.title: This FOSS tool searches inside your files, not just their names, and it changed how I find things on my PC
item.itunes:title: This FOSS tool searches inside your files, not just their names, and it changed how I find things on my PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
File search leaves a lot to be desired these days, especially on Windows. I've leaned on the likes of Everything by voidtools for years, but always wanted a Linux equivalent that didn't require typing a full-on grep command and waiting for it to finish. Recoll is exactly what I was looking for: it's a free and open-source full-text search engine that indexes your entire machine. It obviously grants you the ability to search for files, but it also enables you to search for what's inside them as well. It completely changed the way I search for files on both Linux and Windows, and I don't think I can go back to the default way.

This free self-hosted file explorer links all of my storage into one web-based UI

I set up a self-hosted file manager that lets me browse local drives, cloud storage, and network shares, all from one clean web interface.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

It searches inside your files

Not just what they're named

Recoll gives you far more than just another search box; it's more akin to a query language with field-qualified filters, and even that is just scratching the surface. You can use clauses like "dir:" to search for anything under a given path which includes subdirectories. You can also stack several of them and negate them by adding a minus to exclude certain results. You can "mime:" a result to search by file-type, use wildcards as you'd expect, and filter by size, date—essentially all the operators you'd want.

Recoll also tracks an MD5 checksum for every document it indexes, which is what's behind its power to collapse duplicate results. Turning it on gives you an easy way to track down duplicates all over your machine, which is genuinely useful for cleaning space.

This Docker container converts any file to any format, so I stopped trusting sketchy websites with my private documents

The privacy improvement alone was worth it

6
By  Ayush Pande

The index can be separate to the files

Recoll's indexing can be decoupled from the actual search GUI

Credit: Recoll (GitHub)

The utility of Recoll is pretty clear when it's used on a single desktop, but one of its most interesting features is one that makes it useful across two or more.

The indexer is a standalone program you can run from cron on a schedule, or leave running as a filesystem monitoring daemon that updates the index in real time as files change. Which paths get indexed is up to you, and can be configured to your liking in a plain text config file.

This is what makes it extremely valuable when attached to something like a NAS, if you can give it access. With the Python web front-end, you can search, preview, and download over HTTP. Instead of maintaining an index on every client, you can just run Recoll on the host and search over the web like a search engine for your own files.

5 best free software for searching files on Windows

Search for files on Windows easily with these five free software tools. They also offer advanced features for instant search results.

8
By  Sammy Ekaran

It's not much of a file manager

Disk management is not a strong suit

Recoll is an excellent tool for finding what's inside files, but it's not a file manager, and it doesn't claim to be. There's no treemap, no sorting by size in a directory view, no drive summaries, and there's a real cost to that first round of indexing. That first index of a large collection of files is quite a heavy CPU task, not to mention the size of the index itself. Running it in the background isn't what I would consider light, although most systems should be able to handle it. You can also schedule the on-going indexing, so it's not happening when you least want it to.

Then there's the look of it: it absolutely looks its age compared to a modern search bar, and it's not going to win any design awards. Compared to Everything on Windows, if you're just trying to find the files and not necessarily what's inside them, the former works a lot better. It's also very clearly a Linux-first application, just judging by the "name your price" nature that the Windows version is available for.

8 ways you can optimize Everything to easily find all your files

Optimize your file searches with Everything using advanced filters, indexing, and more to quickly locate files and enhance your workflow efficiency

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Recoll is an excellent way to find what you're looking for on your system

If your drives are tidy and you always know where things are, Recoll will feel like a solution to a problem you don't have. If you've accumulated years of files across multiple machines and several half-finished reorganization attempts, it's a thousand-percent worth a download. Install it, point it at a directory (or an entire system) that you're unsure about, and then query away. It will find exactly what you're looking for and does it with all the tools a power user could ever need.

item.title: I spent $150 on studio headphones before realizing my motherboard was the problem
item.itunes:title: I spent $150 on studio headphones before realizing my motherboard was the problem
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Sometimes, even with a premium pair of studio headphones, plugging them into your motherboard's 3.5 mm audio jack yields sound that's either surprisingly quiet, thin, and bass-starved or aggressively harsh, with digital clipping at high system volumes. Many users might assume onboard PC audio is complete garbage, then open Amazon and drop hundreds of dollars on an external USB DAC/amp stack. However, a lot of modern mid- to high-end motherboards don't just have a basic digital-to-analog converter. High-tier Realtek audio codecs ship with integrated dual operational amplifiers capable of driving loads up to 600 Ω. The problem isn't the lack of onboard power; it's a faulty impedance auto-sensing circuit.

Your motherboard's audio software has quietly categorized your headphones under the wrong impedance tier, leaving the op-amp stuck in the wrong gain stage and making everything sound awful. It might be time to audit your motherboard's audio controller. Manually calibrating your headphone impedance unlocks the full power of the silicone already on your PCB.

My TV's built-in speakers sounded horrible until I changed these 5 settings

It turns out the default speakers aren't as terrible as I thought

By  Tanveer Singh

Your motherboard might be the problem

It might be categorizing your headphones wrong

For a typical enthusiast motherboard, the codec/DAC converts 1s and 0s into low-level analog signals with signal-to-noise ratios pushing 120 dB+. The integrated operational amplifier, sometimes called the op-amp, boosts the voltage and current to drive physical speaker cones.

After considering these components, the next step is looking at the rear I/O versus the front panel header. On almost all motherboards, the dedicated high-power headphone amplifier circuit is routed exclusively to either the rear lime green 3.5 mm jack or the front panel audio header jack, sometimes referred to as HD audio. This means that there actually is a right jack to plug your headphones into. Plugging high-impedance studio cans into the wrong port routes audio through an unamplified line-out buffer designed for powered desktop speakers, starving the drivers of the required voltage swing.

Modern motherboard software suites, whether that's Realtek Audio Console, ASUS Sonic Studio, or Gigabyte Realtek HD Audio Manager, include a smart headphone amp or auto-impedance sensing. This means when you plug a 3.5 mm jack in, the codec sends a tiny DC test pulse down the line, measures resistance across the voice coil, and then categorizes the load into gain tiers. This can cause failure, as it might not sense your headset or headphones as the correct tier. There's low impedance, which is normally IEMs and standard gaming headsets; medium impedance, which is most consumer over-ear headphones; and lastly, high impedance, which demands studio monitoring cans.

Your sound quality won't be at its peak

You might notice some issues

If your headphones or headset are incorrectly categorized, this can lead to major performance dips and, essentially, make your audio feel broken. If your headphones are falsely categorized as low impedance when they're not, then this can lead to underdriving high-impedance cans. This can normally occur if you plug in your headphones while the audio is already playing or via an extension cable. The sensing circuit frequency misreaches the DC resistance as low impedance and then locks the hardware into low gain. As a result, maxing Windows volume to 100% barely yields comfortable listening levels. Bass dynamics sound completely hollow, transients lack punch, and the digital volume slider pushes the DAC into digital clipping.

On the other hand, you might have a false high where you are overdriving sensitive IEMs. Low-impedance multi-driver in-ear monitors or magnetic headphones often present low DC resistance but complex reactive loads. If the software misfires and toggles extreme gain, it can push high voltage into sensitive drivers. As a result, you'll get an audible hissing electronic noise floor at idle, dangerous volume spikes that blow your ears out at 15% system volume, and high harmonic distortion.

How to repair these problems

A simple setting adjustment can make a major difference

Luckily, if you are facing this issue, there is a way to audit and calibrate your onboard amp. The first thing is to check your physical port routing by consulting your motherboard manual or manufacturer's spec sheet. This can help you understand whether the dedicated headphone amplifier drives the rear out or the front panel audio header. That way you know exactly which jack you should be using. On many ASUS and MSI boards, the Auto Sensing Amplifier circuit is tied strictly to the front audio header. Plug directly into the front chassis jack to test.

Next, install the vendor-specific audio console. Generic Microsoft UAA audio drivers can strip away gain controls, whereas proper motherboard packages like the Realtek Audio Console from the Microsoft Store via your motherboard support page give you a lot more control.

Next, it's time to manually override the headphone power amp. Open up your Realtek Audio Console and then go to Device Advanced Settings and locate the headphone power amp setting. Sometimes, this can be labeled as Amplify Level, Smart Headphone Amp, or Impedance Sensing. If your headphones are detected as Level 1 when they're actually 250Ω headphones, then manually click the dropdown and select Level 3 Extreme.

Don't leave your audio quality in the dust

Sometimes the fix takes a couple of minutes

PC enthusiasts spend hours overclocking memory timings, undervolting GPUs, and configuring fan curves to squeeze out 3% more performance. Yet thousands of builders plug $150 studio headphones into an unconfigured, throttled onboard amplifier and accept degraded sound.

Sometimes the issue isn't the headphones; it's your PC itself, or even the port you're plugging them into. You can fix this by checking your manual and opening your motherboard's audio control panel. Adjust your amp gain settings to match your headphones' impedance specs, and you might be surprised to find your audio hardware delivers significantly better performance.

item.title: My old phone is the best dash cam I own, and it uploads the clips when I get home
item.itunes:title: My old phone is the best dash cam I own, and it uploads the clips when I get home
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As an enthusiast, I have plenty of older smartphones. Many are too old to be a daily driver, but still useful enough to find a purpose, and I'm always looking for interesting projects to put them to use. So, recently, I turned one of them into a dashcam.

You might find the idea strange, but hear me out. For one, I was looking for an interesting project. But more than that, I didn't want to spend money on a new dashcam. Instead, I mounted an old Android phone in the car, installed Droid Dashcam, and connected it to a USB charger.

The app handles all dashcam duties, saves recordings to the phone, and I've set it up to automatically back up over Wi-Fi. It's basically a fully hands-off setup. I just drive; the phone records footage, and it saves everything to the cloud. All for free, using hardware I already had. It's better than any dashcam I've owned.

Droid Dashcam turns an old phone into a proper dashcam

Automatic recordings and looped storage use

Credit: 

As part of the project, I first needed an app that could turn the phone into a dashcam. The simplest approach would be to just leave the camera running, but what's the fun in that? I wanted a solution that could save data, GPS information, and more, just like a real dashcam. That's where Droid Dashcam fits in.

The app offers an extensive feature set that turns your phone into a dashcam. This includes essentials like continuous loop recording, so you can let it record through an entire drive without filling up your phone's storage. It's an essential feature that lets you configure a storage limit. Once it reaches the storage limit, the app automatically deletes older recordings and makes room for newer ones, which is exactly how I want my phone-based dashcam to behave.

The other feature that seals the deal, as far as dashcam capabilities are concerned, is that the app can start recording automatically when the phone is connected to power, plus a range of other triggers. This makes a lot of sense, since I don't want to tap the start button every time. You can set it to charging as a trigger, or even a Bluetooth connection. This means that when your car switches on, Droid Dashcam considers it as a cue to initiate recording.

The footage is only useful if it has the right context

Metadata like date, speed, and GPS make the footage useful

Remember what I mentioned earlier about wanting a true dashcam-style experience? Well, this app can achieve that. In fact, it can overlay proper date and time stamps in addition to GPS coordinates, speed, and even vehicle registration information if you choose to embed that in the video. The purpose of a dashcam is to provide proof if something goes wrong, so this information isn't optional in my books.

If I'm going to contest a speeding ticket, I need to prove I wasn't speeding. That can only happen when I have proof of speed embedded within the video. Now, recording footage is just one part of the equation. That footage also needs to be easily accessible. This is when using a phone as a dashcam becomes surprisingly useful. Unlike dashcams, phones are fully connected devices that let you add apps.

Droid Dashcam stores the recordings locally. But I can save those files wherever I want. For example, I can tell Google Photos to back up that device folder, which means the moment I park and my phone connects to Wi-Fi, it automatically uploads the footage to Google Photos. Not only does it serve as a backup, but it also lets me easily view the footage from any device or computer.

The obvious tradeoff is that hours of 4K footage take a lot of storage, so backing this up to the cloud can quickly fill up your cloud locker. That's why I prefer uploading this footage to a NAS instead. The workflow is largely the same: use your choice of FTP sync app, or a tool like Syncthing, and point it to the folder on your phone. The moment I connect to Wi-Fi, this data syncs to my NAS. This means my footage is backed up, and I don't need to pay for cloud storage either.

All that to say, with the right approach, the entire setup is as hands-free as it gets.

A simple way to reuse a phone rather than buying a dedicated dashcam

Look, a dedicated dashcam will always make more sense for most people. It's purpose-built for the job, handles heat better, and suits car installation better. But if you've got a spare phone lying around, all it takes is installing an app from the Play Store to build your own dashcam. With the right tweaks, the workflow is nearly invisible, making it a great way to reuse existing hardware.

Droid Dashcam

The Droid Dashcam app lets you turn any Android phone into a full-fledged dashcam.

See at Google Play Store

Droid Dashcam stores the recordings locally. But I can save those files wherever I want. For example, I can tell Google Photos to back up that device folder, which means the moment I park and my phone connects to Wi-Fi, it automatically uploads the footage to Google Photos. Not only does it serve as a backup, but it also lets me easily view the footage from any device or computer.

The obvious tradeoff is that hours of 4K footage take a lot of storage, so backing this up to the cloud can quickly fill up your cloud locker. That's why I prefer uploading this footage to a NAS instead. The workflow is largely the same: use your choice of FTP sync app, or a tool like Syncthing, and point it to the folder on your phone. The moment I connect to Wi-Fi, this data syncs to my NAS. This means my footage is backed up, and I don't need to pay for cloud storage either.

All that to say, with the right approach, the entire setup is as hands-free as it gets.

Look, a dedicated dashcam will always make more sense for most people. It's purpose-built for the job, handles heat better, and suits car installation better. But if you've got a spare phone lying around, all it takes is installing an app from the Play Store to build your own dashcam. item.itunes:summary:
I spent my early 3D printing days creating aesthetically pleasing models and messing around with slicer settings. So, it didn’t take too long before I started to grow tired of printing every cosplay item, desk accessory, and figurine I’d find online. That’s when I stumbled into the rabbit hole of functional prints – models that have a practical utility beyond simply adorning my living space.

Although I'm particularly fond of the 3D printed tripod mounts and Raspberry Pi MIPI latches, custom cable management tools are the ones I rely on the most when it comes to functional prints. In fact, I daresay my home lab would have devolved into a disorganized cable clutter if I had to rely on aftermarket solutions instead of custom models I created over the years with my 3D printer.

3D printing saved me money, but only after I stopped printing “solutions”

I had to stop printing novelty “solutions” and focus instead on durable replacements.

24
By  Jeff Butts

Desk clips, grommets, and wire channels keep my home lab cable chaos in check

They’re also fairly inexpensive to print

Between my tendency to grab old hardware at flea markets and all the new paraphernalia I receive for reviews, my home lab has wires running all over the place. After all, each machine needs its own set of power and Ethernet cables, with GUI-laden everyday systems like my gaming laptop and test benches needing display output and keyboard + mouse cables. The cables by my microcontrollers and KVM docks only contribute to this clutter.

So, I 3D printed a bunch of accessories to tackle my cable chaos. For my everyday machines, I ended up installing clips around the desks, so I can attach the unneeded cables at designated spots instead of leaving them dangling when I’m no longer using them. Power and Ethernet cables, in particular, get routed through the grommets I 3D printed for my desks, but I also run longer cables, like the one connecting my KVM dock to all my test benches, through them.

I’ve also got my eye on grid systems for some under-the-table routing. But truth be told, I only ever printed two of the smaller models to route a select few cables instead of covering the underside of my desk with a carefully planned grid setup.

Then you’ve got the cable channels, which I adore to bits. Even with all the grommets and desk clips, my cable management efforts would be pointless if I just left the entire pile of wires running all over the floor and into the other rooms. Since cable channels conceal these wires, I can just place them on the side of the wall, and with most models being easy to scale, I can modify their dimensions within the slicer as I see fit.

But I’ve also got a handful of 3D prints managing the cables inside my PCs

Tiny cable combs were a godsend for my home servers

Since I can’t just lay cable channels inside the cramped space within my server rigs and gaming machines, I had to opt for tinier 3D-printed solutions. Smaller combs are pretty effective at grouping similar sets of wires. Likewise, I’ve made a bunch of tiny snap-on cable clips that stick to my PC case and keep wires close together (and to ensure I don’t have stray wire segments touching the cabinet fans).

I’ve also made a PSU shroud bracket for one of my server rigs, as its non-modular power supply makes the front connections look rather messy. And while they aren’t strictly associated with managing cables, my screw trays help out quite a lot by ensuring I don’t lose those pesky motherboard screws when I’m mounting new accessories to the PC.

5 3D prints I actually use daily

Five practical 3D prints I rely on every day, from drawer organization to desk-friendly gear storage that actually sticks.

6
By  Jeff Butts

I rely on PETG for my cable management tools

But TPU and (to some extent) PLA+ have their perks for certain prints

When it comes to the filament, I stick with PETG for the most part and avoid PLA like the plague for anything that goes inside my PCs. After all, the latter is prone to softening and warping at somewhat high temperatures, and even though my server rigs have decent ambient temps for the most part, they’re not cool enough to ensure my PLA prints don't get damaged over time. PLA is also pretty ineffective for cable management accessories where there’s always some mechanical stress on the print, as it becomes brittle when it’s subjected to a lot of force.

PETG, on the other hand, is great for printing accessories that keep the cables secure inside self-hosting server rigs, and its ability to resist constant mechanical strength makes it pretty effective for cable clips that hold wires at 90° angles. That said, I typically use TPU for grommets, and PLA+ isn’t a terrible option for cable channels that aren’t exposed to a lot of heat and mechanical stress.

The best part? Most of the prints, barring huge PLA+ cable channels, barely need more than 20 grams of filament. Even if I were to print a dozen more of these models, I wouldn't need more than a single PETG spool.
